unknowns: day_f_min / day_f_max / night_f_min / night_f_max: no admissible source frames a controlled day/night temperature target for this species -- every source treats it only as an uncultivated wild weed to identify and remove, describing habitat and geographic origin, not a cultivation temperature range.

chill_damage_f / cool_rest_note: no admissible source gives any cold-hardiness figure, hardiness-zone rating, or dormancy/chilling requirement for this species at all -- unlike many cultivated species' NC State Plant Toolbox pages, this species' entry has no Hardiness Zone field, so there is nothing to even mis-map onto a damage-onset number.
humidity_need / humidity_pct_min / humidity_pct_max: no admissible source addresses ambient humidity for this outdoor wild plant.

light_fc_min / light_fc_good / direct_sun_hours_max: NC State's Light field gives only duration-band categories (Full sun 6+ hrs, Partial Shade 2-6 hrs), not footcandle figures. direct_sun_hours_max was left null rather than using the 2-6 hr partial-shade figure, because full_sun is also endorsed unconditionally for this species and applying the narrower band's hour ceiling would misrepresent the full-sun option -- the same overstatement risk documented in this catalog's other wild/toxic-species records (e.g. Poison Ivy).

soil_base: no admissible source frames growing conditions in container or garden-bed cultivation terms for this uncultivated species. The only soil-adjacent structured field on NC State's page is the bare 'Soil Drainage: Moist' Cultural Conditions tag, which was used for soil_drainage but does not itself describe a soil mix/base, so soil_base was left null. No source discusses potting mix, bed amendment, or any cultivation-specific soil framing for this weed.

soil_ph_min / soil_ph_max: no admissible source gives a Soil pH field for this species at all -- unlike many other NC State Plant Toolbox pages, this species' page has no 'Soil pH' entry, and no other admissible source addresses pH.

water_regime / water_dry_down_target / water_check_depth_cm / water_growing_days_est / water_dormant_days_est / water_estimate_basis: no admissible source frames watering guidance for this wild, un-irrigated, uncontained plant. NC State's 'Soil Drainage: Moist' field (used for soil_drainage) describes the native habitat's soil character, not an active watering instruction, so it was not extended to fill any water_* field.

fertilize_active_months / fertilize_interval_days / fertilize_strength: no admissible source addresses fertilizing a plant that every source treats only as a weed to identify and remove, never to cultivate.

toxic_to_pets: grounded solely in NC State's own 'Problem for Cats' and 'Problem for Dogs' Problems tags (and the matching '#problem for dogs' / '#problem for cats' page tags), which name cats and dogs specifically. No admissible source gives a pet-specific dose, symptom list, or clinical outcome distinct from the human-scoped block described in toxicity_detail. UMD's 'toxic to humans and to livestock' and Penn State's 'toxic to humans and other animals' language is broader than humans-only but does not itself name cats or dogs, so per this task's own rule it was treated only as corroborating general toxicity, not as independent support for toxic_to_pets.

toxicity_detail: NC State's most detailed poisoning data -- 'Poison Severity: High', the full symptom list ('Salivation, vomiting, diarrhea, muscular weakness, paralysis, nervousness, trembling, dilation of pupils, weak pulse, convulsions, coma'), 'Poison Toxic Principle', and 'Poison Part' -- is nested specifically under a 'Poisonous to Humans' heading on that page, the same structural pattern this task's own guidance warns about. That symptom list is therefore not presented as pet-specific symptom evidence; NC State was cited only for the toxic principle and affected-parts facts, which are independently corroborated by Penn State's and UMD's species-level, non-human-exclusive language. No admissible source gives a pet-specific ('for cats' / 'for dogs') symptom description or dose threshold.

toxicity_detail -- livestock-specific dose figures excluded: Penn State's quoted toxicosis thresholds (0.25% of body weight fresh-weight material for horses, 0.5% for cattle) and UGA Cooperative Extension's 'Toxic Weeds and Trees in Horse Pastures' framing ('It is also toxic to horses, but they have to consume more of this compared to water hemlock for it to be lethal') are explicitly scoped to horses/cattle, not cats or dogs, so neither was folded into toxicity_detail or used to support toxic_to_pets. UGA's companion 'Identifying Toxic Weeds in Georgia Pastures and Hayfields' publication states only that 'All animals are susceptible to the piperidine alkaloids' in a livestock-pasture context that goes on to discuss 'calf, foal' outcomes -- an unscoped 'all animals' statement that, per this task's own rule, does not name cats or dogs and so was not used to support toxic_to_pets.

name_note left null: no admissible source disputes the accepted binomial. NC State and RHS each anchor to Conium maculatum via their own structured Genus/Species and Name Status fields respectively, and no admissible source lists a different accepted binomial. Multiple common-name synonyms exist (NC State: Deadly Hemlock, Poison Fool's Parsley, Poison Parsley, Spotted Parsley; RHS: California fern, cashes, cegiden, herb bennet, Nebraska fern, poison parsley, snakeweed, spotted hemlock, spotted parsley, St Benedict's herb, winter fern) but this is ordinary common-name variety, not a scientific-name conflict, so it was not treated as a name_note-worthy dispute.

unknowns identification_confusion: the identification-confusion pattern with edible relatives -- a documented poisoning-risk pattern -- is well supported across every admissible source that addresses it. NC State's Plant Toolbox carries a structured 'is often confused with' field naming Angelica archangelica, Daucus carota (wild carrot / Queen Anne's lace), Heracleum mantegazzianum (giant hogweed), Heracleum maximum (cow parsnip), Pastinaca sativa (wild parsnip), Petroselinum crispum (parsley), and Pimpinella anisum (anise), plus a separate 'Similar but less problematic plants' list (Daucus carota, Daucus carota subsp. sativus, Pastinaca sativa). RHS states: 'Its lacy white umbels have often led to victims making the fatal mistake of confusing hemlock with its innocent cousins, such as parsley, carrot or fennel.' Penn State states: 'Wild carrot (also called Queen Anne's lace), wild parsnip, spotted water hemlock, and purple-stemmed angelica can sometimes be confused with these species because they are in the same family and have some similar features,' and separately that the plant's 'overall appearance resembles carrot and parsley.' UMD states the species 'is sometimes mistaken for one of its crop relatives' (carrots, celery, parsnips) and 'is also commonly mistaken for Queen Anne's Lace (Daucus carota).' None of this maps to a schema field, so it is documented here rather than forced into one.

unknowns historical_note: RHS and Penn State both independently note the species' historical association with the execution of the philosopher Socrates in 399 BC by drinking poison hemlock -- notable context with no matching schema field, documented here rather than fabricated into one.

unknowns source-coverage gap: Clemson Cooperative Extension HGIC (hgic.clemson.edu) and UF/IFAS Extension (edis.ifas.ufl.edu / ask.ifas.ufl.edu) were both searched specifically and repeatedly for Conium maculatum / poison hemlock content; no admissible page addressing this species was found on either domain. UF/IFAS's own 'Common Poisonous Weed and Invasive Plant Species in Florida Residential Landscapes' (EP631) survey article was directly fetched and confirmed not to mention Conium maculatum, poison hemlock, or coniine anywhere in its text. Missouri Botanical Garden (missouribotanicalgarden.org / plantfinder.mobot.org) was also searched with no admissible page found for this species, consistent with MOBOT's Plant Finder being oriented toward cultivated ornamentals rather than roadside weeds.

is_houseplant: no admissible source explicitly states poison hemlock is not grown indoors (unsurprising, since none discusses indoor/container culture for it at all). Set to false based on the complete absence of any houseplant/container-culture guidance across all admissible sources consulted, combined with NC State's explicit 'Weed' Plant Type tag and every source's uniform framing of the species as something to identify and remove rather than cultivate.

name_note — removed on audit: The record stores name_note as the JSON string "null" (quoted) rather than an actual JSON null, which is exactly the defect structural check 6 warns about. Every other genuinely-unresolved field in the record (day_f_min, chill_damage_f, water_regime, etc.) is correctly encoded as a bare null, making this a one-off encoding bug rather than a formatting convention. As written, a strict parser would treat name_note as a populated string field with no supporting citation, which also fails check 1 (no citation's claim label contains 'name_note' or literally supports the string "null").

is_houseplant — removed on audit: The only citation offered (NC State's 'Plant Type: Herbaceous Perennial, Perennial, Poisonous, Weed' tag list) does not literally state that the species is not grown as a houseplant -- it only categorizes plant type. is_houseplant=false is an inference from the absence of any indoor/container-culture discussion across all admissible sources, not a directly quoted fact. Per the per-field check ('Does the quote ACTUALLY state this value?'), this citation does not carry the weight the claim label assigns it, even though the inferred value itself is very likely correct in reality for a documented invasive roadside weed.

toxicity_detail — removed on audit: The opening sentence claims the species is 'rated highly toxic by every admissible source that addresses toxicity,' but I fetched all four cited pages directly and only NC State's Poisonous to Humans section literally uses a formal severity rating ('Poison Severity: High') and the phrase 'HIGHLY TOXIC.' Penn State's two pages and UMD's page describe the plant as 'toxic,' 'poisonous,' and 'can be fatal' but do not use a rating scale or the word 'highly' -- so 'rated ... by every admissible source' overstates uniformity of characterization. This is a framing overreach in the summary sentence; the substantive mechanism/symptom/affected-parts content later in the field is accurately quoted and appropriately hedged (it correctly declines to present NC State's human-scoped symptom list as pet evidence).

records.name_note: RHS's Plant Profile (taxon ID 40530, page titled "Hibiscus syriacus | rose of Sharon") gives an explicit "Name Status: Correct" determination for the plain binomial Hibiscus syriacus. This is unlike the sibling species Hibiscus rosa-sinensis already in this catalog, where RHS's own database is internally split between the plain and ×-marked forms. No admissible source (NC State, Missouri Botanical Garden, Clemson, UF/IFAS, Penn State, Maryland, UGA) disputes Hibiscus syriacus as the correct name for this species; NC State's "Previously known as" field lists only historical synonyms (Althaea frutex, Hibiscus acerifolius, Ketmia syriaca), consistent with, not contradicting, RHS's determination.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension's structured tags read "non-toxic for cats," "non-toxic for dogs," and "non-toxic for horses" for this species, and the page carries no Poison or Poisonous-to-Humans section at all. No other admissible source (RHS, Missouri Botanical Garden, Clemson, UGA) mentions toxicity for this species in either direction.
unknowns: day_f_min/day_f_max/night_f_min/night_f_max: no admissible source gives an ambient day/night temperature range for this species; only winter hardiness-zone survival data was found (see chill_damage_f note).

chill_damage_f: no admissible source gives an actionable frost-damage-onset temperature. All four sources that address cold hardiness give winter-SURVIVAL zone/banding ratings rather than a damage-onset figure for the growing plant: NC State's "USDA Plant Hardiness Zone: 5a, 5b, 6a, 6b, 7a, 7b, 8a, 8b, 9a, 9b"; Missouri Botanical Garden's "Zone: 5 to 8"; Clemson's "hardy in USDA Zones 5-9"; and RHS's UK hardiness rating "H5" ("hardy in most places throughout the UK even in severe winters (-15 to -10)"). Per instructions these survival ratings were not mapped onto this damage-onset field, and RHS's figure would additionally require a °C-to-°F unit conversion not licensed by the no-synthesis rule.

cool_rest_note: no admissible source discusses an indoor dormancy/cool-rest period. This species is a fully in-ground, winter-hardy deciduous shrub that loses its leaves and goes dormant outdoors each year (confirmed by NC State's "Deciduous" leaf characteristic and RHS's "Foliage: Deciduous"), not a container/houseplant with an indoor cool-rest regime as documented elsewhere in this catalog for tropical Hibiscus rosa-sinensis.
humidity_need/humidity_pct_min/humidity_pct_max: no admissible source addresses ambient humidity requirements for this outdoor landscape shrub.
light_fc_min/light_fc_good: no admissible source gives a foot-candle light measurement for this species.

direct_sun_hours_max: NC State's "Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)" defines the floor for its Full Sun category, not a ceiling for this species; no admissible source gives an upper-bound sun-hours figure.

soil_drainage: left null despite multiple sources discussing drainage, because the phrasing is genuinely ambiguous and does not cleanly map onto the schema's fast/moderate/moisture_retentive categories. NC State's own structured Soil Drainage tags for this species list "Good Drainage," "Moist," "Occasionally Dry," AND "Occasionally Wet" together (i.e., NC State itself tags the species tolerant of both occasional dryness and occasional wetness); Missouri Botanical Garden separately describes "average, medium moisture, well-drained soils... tolerates poor soils and some drought"; and RHS phrases Moisture as a disjunction, "Moist but well–drained or Well–drained." This mirrors a combination this catalog's own prior audit already rejected mapping to a single category for the sibling species Hibiscus rosa-sinensis on the same grounds, so the same caution is applied here rather than forcing a category.

soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max: no admissible source gives a numeric pH range. NC State states only that the species "is pH adaptable" (no bounds), and RHS gives only a categorical descriptor, "pH: Acid or Neutral," with no numbers -- consistent with how this catalog treated the identical RHS categorical-pH pattern for Hibiscus rosa-sinensis.

water_regime: no admissible source frames watering for this species in terms of the schema's container-oriented categories (keep_moist/dry_surface_between/dry_thoroughly_between/keep_barely_moist). Missouri Botanical Garden's "Water: Medium" is a bare categorical tag with no elaboration, and NC State's description ("It grows best in moist, well-drained soils but is tolerant of all except extremely wet or dry soils") is a garden soil-moisture preference, not a watering instruction.

water_dry_down_target/water_check_depth_cm/water_growing_days_est/water_dormant_days_est/water_estimate_basis: no admissible source gives a watering frequency in days, a moisture-check depth, or a dry-down target; consistent with this being an in-ground landscape shrub/small tree rather than a container plant in any admissible source.

fertilize_active_months/fertilize_interval_days/fertilize_strength: no admissible source (NC State, Missouri Botanical Garden, Clemson, RHS, UGA) specifies a fertilizing schedule, dilution strength, or feeding calendar for Hibiscus syriacus.

UF/IFAS: this species has a dedicated UF/IFAS publication (ENH454/ST295, "Hibiscus syriacus: Rose-of-Sharon"), but as of this research its edis.ifas.ufl.edu/ask.ifas.ufl.edu page returns HTTP 410 Gone ("The publication you requested is no longer available on Ask IFAS") -- it has been retired from the live admissible domain and was therefore not usable as a source. No other edis.ifas.ufl.edu or ask.ifas.ufl.edu page substantively addressing this species' care was found (only incidental host-plant mentions in unrelated insect-pest publications).

Penn State Extension and University of Maryland Extension: both domains mention this species only in passing (Penn State: a juglone-tolerance plant list; Maryland: pest pages for hibiscus sawfly and armored scale, and a deer-resistance list) -- none of these pages give care/cultivation data usable for any field in this record.

unknowns: day_f_min, day_f_max, night_f_min, night_f_max: no admissible source gives ambient day/night temperature ranges for this outdoor deciduous landscape tree; only winter cold-hardiness zone/rating data exists (NC State: USDA zones 4a-9b; MOBOT: zone 4 to 9; UF/IFAS 'Burgundy' cultivar sheet: zones 4B through 9A; RHS: hardiness rating H6, 'hardy in all of UK and northern Europe (-20 to -15)'), which does not map to this field.

light_fc_min, light_fc_good: no admissible source gives foot-candle light values for this species.

fertilize_active_months, fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_strength: no admissible source discusses a fertilizing schedule, frequency, or product strength for this species.

toxic_to_pets, toxicity_detail: none of the admissible sources consulted for this species -- NC State Plant Toolbox, Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder, Clemson HGIC's Magnolia factsheet and its dedicated 'Pet Owners Beware: 11 Poisonous Houseplants' article, RHS's plant profile, UF/IFAS EDIS fact sheets for the species and several cultivars (ST386/ST388/ST389/FP368/FP370/FP371/FP373), UGA Extension's 'Landscape Plants for Georgia' guide and its two dedicated pet-toxic-plant news articles, and Penn State Extension's 'spring plants that are poisonous to horses, dogs, and barn cats' article -- name Magnolia x soulangeana, or magnolias generally, in connection with toxicity to any animal.

records.cool_rest_note: European plums need roughly 700-1,100 chilling hours (time spent between 32°F and 45°F) to come out of dormancy and bloom efficiently -- more than the 500-900 hours Japanese plums require, per UGA Cooperative Extension, which explicitly names "European plums" (not the genus generically) for this figure.
unknowns: day_f_min/day_f_max/night_f_min/night_f_max/humidity_need/humidity_pct_min/humidity_pct_max/light_fc_min/light_fc_good: no admissible source discusses this species in indoor/greenhouse/container-microclimate terms; it is treated purely as an outdoor orchard/landscape tree, so no ambient temperature, humidity, or footcandle figures exist to record.

direct_sun_hours_max: NC State's Light field states only a minimum ('Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)') with no stated maximum, so left null rather than treating the minimum as a ceiling.

chill_damage_f: left null. No admissible source gives a single actionable frost/cold damage-onset temperature for this species. Penn State Extension's 'Orchard Frost - Critical Temperatures for Various Fruits' page (used elsewhere in this catalog for peach, apple, pear, sweet cherry, and apricot) does not include plum in its table at all. The only cold-related figures found are USDA hardiness-zone survival ranges (NC State: zones 4a-9b) and RHS's Hardiness rating H5 ('hardy in most places throughout the UK even in severe winters,' -15 to -10°C), which are survival/tolerance floors, not damage-onset points, and a winter-chilling dormancy REQUIREMENT (see cool_rest_note) which is a different concept from frost damage onset.

water_regime/water_dry_down_target/water_check_depth_cm/water_growing_days_est/water_dormant_days_est/water_estimate_basis: this is a harm-capable field. Only qualitative guidance was found -- UGA: 'Supply plenty of moisture during the summer months and well into the fall, since fall in Georgia is prone to periods of episodic drought'; RHS: 'Irrigate in dry periods.' Neither source gives a specific regime (moist vs. dry-between), a check-depth, a day-interval figure, or a quantifiable amount (e.g. gallons), so none of these fields, including the free-text basis field, could be populated without inferring beyond what was stated.

fertilize_active_months/fertilize_interval_days/fertilize_strength: left null. UGA and Clemson both give granular fertilizer schedules (lb of 10-10-10 and calcium nitrate/ammonium nitrate) rather than a day-interval figure or liquid-dilution 'strength' framing, AND the exact months differ by tree age in a way that is not consistent between the two sources -- UGA: Year 1 = March (10-10-10), May and July (calcium nitrate); Year 2 = March (10-10-10), July (calcium nitrate). Clemson: March (10-10-10) and August (calcium nitrate/ammonium nitrate) scaled by tree age, PLUS 'additional nitrogen in mid-May and mid-July.' Given this age-dependent variation and the cross-source inconsistency in which calendar months apply, no single species-wide month list is safely supportable, consistent with how this catalog handled the same first-year-vs-mature-tree ambiguity for Peach.

toxic_to_pets/toxicity_detail: toxic_to_pets true rests on NC State's bare 'Problem for Cats' / 'Problem for Dogs' tags (present on the plain species page itself). The only elaborated mechanism/symptom/toxic-part text found is nested under a 'Poisonous to Humans' heading on the related 'Stanley' cultivar page (same species, Prunus domestica) -- the plain species page has no poison section of its own at all. That human-scoped detail was kept in toxicity_detail but explicitly labeled as human-targeted rather than presented as pet-specific, per this catalog's convention (see Peach). No admissible source gives a dog/cat-specific symptom list, toxic dose, or severity rating for this species.

UF/IFAS coverage: UF/IFAS's plum-related EDIS content ('Growing Plums in Florida', HS895) covers only University of Florida's own low-chill 'Gulf' series cultivars, which are explicitly Japanese-type plums (Prunus salicina hybrids), not Prunus domestica -- so it was not used for this species-specific record.

soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max: RHS's own structured 'pH' field gives only the broad category 'Acid or Neutral' (and NC State's categorical field for the 'Stanley' cultivar gives 'Acid (<6.0)' and 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)'), while RHS's own Cultivation prose, Clemson, and UGA all independently give the same specific numeric target (6.0-6.5 / 6.5); the specific figure was used and the broader categorical tags were not merged in, consistent with how this catalog treated the same broad-tag-vs-specific-figure pattern for Apple and Peach.

toxicity_detail — removed on audit: The cited quote (NC State 'Stanley' cultivar page) is explicitly headed 'Poisonous to Humans' -- verified live, that page has no 'Poisonous to Pets' section at all, only bare category tags. The record's own prose concedes this human scoping, but still uses the human symptom/mechanism text (cyanide, 'brick red mucous membranes, dilated pupils, difficulty breathing, panting, shock') as the toxicity_detail for a record whose toxic_to_pets=true, which fails check 4's requirement that toxicity_detail content actually be about animal toxicity. No admissible source gives any cat/dog-specific symptom, dose, or severity for this species, so this elaborated detail should not stand as the toxicity_detail supporting a pet-toxicity claim.

name_note — removed on audit: Only two claims in this field trace to the citations array (RHS 'Name Status Correct'; NC State's 'Greengage and damson plums are subspecies of P. domestica'). The note goes further and asserts, with no supporting citation anywhere in the array: (1) that RHS's own catalog lists 'Greengage as Prunus domestica subsp. italica' and 'Damson under its own subspecies entries', and (2) that NC State's 'Bluefire' cultivar page also uses the Prunus domestica binomial. Neither claim's label appears in citations and neither is traceable to any quote provided, violating structural check 1 -- these are uncited factual assertions embedded in an otherwise-cited field.

unknowns: day_f_min/day_f_max/night_f_min/night_f_max/humidity_need/humidity_pct_min/humidity_pct_max/light_fc_min/light_fc_good/direct_sun_hours_max: these read as indoor-microclimate and container-culture fields; no admissible source discusses ambient indoor temperature, humidity, or foot-candle/sun-hour ceilings for this outdoor landscape/orchard tree.

chill_damage_f: left null despite finding a Penn State Extension frost-critical-temperature table specifically labeled 'Sweet cherries' -- 10%-kill temperatures range from 17°F at 'first swelling' up to 28°F at 'first bloom' through 'post bloom' (with 90%-kill temperatures ranging 5°F to 25°F across the same nine stages). As with this catalog's treatment of Peach's analogous table, picking any single one of these values to represent 'the' damage-onset temperature would misrepresent a curve as a point, so the field is left null and the full table is preserved in citations instead.

cool_rest_note: left null. Sweet cherry clearly has a real winter-chilling dormancy requirement -- UGA CAES states sweet cherries (except 'Stella') are 'limited to the Piedmont and Mountain sections of Georgia,' implying a meaningfully high chilling need -- but no admissible source gives sweet cherry itself a specific chill-hour figure. The only concrete chill-hour number found anywhere in this research (1,000 to 2,000 hr) is UGA's own figure for the sibling species sour cherry (Prunus cerasus), stated in a separate sentence explicitly about sour cherry; borrowing that number for Prunus avium would misattribute a different species' figure, so the field stays null rather than repurpose the sibling species' number.

water_regime/water_dry_down_target/water_check_depth_cm/water_growing_days_est/water_dormant_days_est: left null. RHS's own watering guidance splits by tree age and site rather than giving one regime: established in-ground trees 'shouldn't need watering' at all, while young trees and any tree grown in a container need regular supplemental watering, with container trees specifically kept 'evenly moist.' None of this catalog's four water_regime values describes 'no supplemental water for an established in-ground tree,' and the 'evenly moist' language is scoped to container culture, which this record treats as secondary to garden_bed (see soil_base). Rather than force one point onto this age/site-dependent guidance, the enum and its numeric companions are left null, with the qualitative distinction preserved in water_estimate_basis instead.

fertilize_active_months/fertilize_interval_days/fertilize_strength: left null. RHS states in-ground cherry trees 'shouldn't need any additional feeding' under normal mulched conditions and only suggests feeding 'if harvests are particularly poor,' with timing given only as 'early spring' -- not a specific named month that could be translated to a calendar number. A concrete 'every fortnight' / 'April to August' liquid-feed schedule does exist in the same source, but it is explicitly scoped to trees 'growing in containers,' which this record treats as secondary culture for this species (see soil_base/is_houseplant); applying that container schedule as if it were the species' general in-ground fertilizing regimen would misrepresent scoped guidance as universal -- the same category of error this catalog avoided on Peach's UGA first-year-only fertilizer schedule.

is_houseplant: left false. RHS states cherry trees 'crop best in the ground' with container growing offered only as a fallback 'if you don't have suitable soil or an available site,' and frames fruiting itself as needing 'a warm, sheltered spot' outdoors. This is outdoor/container fruit-tree culture, not indoor long-term houseplant use, so is_houseplant stays false, consistent with how this catalog treated Peach's similar RHS container language.

toxicity_detail: left null even though toxic_to_pets is true. NC State's Cats/Dogs/Horses '#problem for' tags are standalone landscape-tag pills, independent of any other section, and directly support toxic_to_pets. But the only detailed toxicity narrative on that page -- Poison Severity ('Medium'), the cyanide-compound symptom description, Poison Toxic Principle ('Cyanogenic glycosides (amygdalin & prunasin)'), and the Poison Part list -- is nested entirely under NC State's own 'Poisonous to Humans:' header, and no admissible source gives any cat/dog-specific symptom or dose information for this species. Populating toxicity_detail from that block would blend human-scoped poisoning data into a field this catalog uses to detail pet risk -- the same error this catalog corrected on Peach's toxicity_detail during audit -- so the field stays null rather than repeat it here.

toxicity_detail seed/pit-vs-fruit distinction (captured per this record's research brief, but not used to populate the field above, for the human/pet-scope reason in the previous entry): NC State's page states 'The leaves, flowers, green fruits, ripe fruits and seeds contain cyanide compounds in detectable quantities, but the seeds and fruit stalks have the highest concentration of toxins. If a couple of pits (stones, which enclose the seeds) are accidentally swallowed, it will not cause poisoning.' The same page separately confirms the fruit itself as 'Fruit edible raw or cooked.' Read together, these establish that the edible part is the fruit flesh, while cyanogenic compounds concentrate specifically in the seed/pit (and fruit stalk) rather than the flesh -- the same seed/pit-vs-flesh distinction this catalog already documents for Peach and Apple -- and this quote is preserved in the citations array for the record even though it cannot populate toxicity_detail itself.

toxic_to_pets: NC State also tags '#problem for horses,' but per this catalog's established convention (see Peach), horses fall outside the toxic_to_pets boolean's scope; true is supported solely by the cats/dogs tags.

soil_base: populated as garden_bed on RHS's own explicit statement that cherry trees 'crop best in the ground,' with container growing presented in the same sentence as a secondary fallback. This is more direct evidence than this catalog required to leave Peach's soil_base null (Peach's only candidate was a bare drainage tag with no in-ground/container statement at all); here the source states a primary substrate outright, so garden_bed is populated rather than left null.

outdoor_sun_exposure: populated as full_sun and part_shade together, not treated as a conflict to resolve. NC State, the RHS species profile, and RHS's cherry-growing guide (which names 'Sweet cherries' specifically, distinguishing them from 'acid cherries' which 'will tolerate some shade') all independently give full_sun. Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder entry for this exact species separately gives 'Sun: Full sun to part shade' as its own tolerance-range field rather than a competing preference claim, so part_shade is added alongside full_sun rather than nulled out as a disagreement.

scientific_name_accepted/name_note: NC State's Prunus avium page carries no 'Previously known as' synonym box, and RHS's own Name Status field for Prunus avium reads 'Correct' with no synonym listed either -- both admissible sources agree with nothing to adjudicate, so scientific_name_accepted is copied over unchanged.

water_estimate_basis — removed on audit: The field's final clause -- 'with container trees kept evenly moist' -- does not trace to citation 17 (or any other citation). Citation 17's quote from RHS 'How to grow cherries' reads only: 'Established cherry trees in open ground shouldn't need watering. Young cherry trees and trees grown in pots will need some additional watering throughout the growing season.' I fetched the live RHS page directly: the 'evenly moist' language is real, but it belongs to a separate, later sentence in the Watering section -- 'Trees in containers need a steady supply of moisture throughout the growing season, so water regularly in dry spells, aiming to keep the compost evenly moist. But never leave them standing in water...' -- which was never quoted or added as its own citation entry. So the field asserts a specific, accurate-but-uncited detail, exactly the traceability defect this same catalog's own audited Peach record (app/data/verified/b28-holly-and-nuts.json, 'water_estimate_basis — removed on audit') establishes as disqualifying: 'the field text includes... [a detail] attributed to [a source], but no citation entry in the array contains this string.' The base watering claim (established in-ground trees need no water; young/container trees need regular watering) is soundly cited; only the added 'evenly moist' clause is unsupported, but per this catalog's own precedent an untraceable addition inside the field's text is grounds to treat the field as unsound as written.

records.name_note: NC State (page titled "Citrus x sinensis") and Missouri Botanical Garden (page titled "Citrus × sinensis") both treat this plant as a hybrid: MoBot states "Citrus sinensis is not a naturally occurring species. Based on genetic analysis, most experts agree that this is a hybrid plant resulting from a purposeful cross between a hybrid mandarin orange (Citrus reticulata) and and a hybrid pomelo (Citrus maxima)," and NC State states "It is a hybrid resulting from a cross between a mandarin orange and a pomelo although when this was done is not fully known." RHS, by contrast, titles the species plainly "Citrus sinensis | sweet orange" with no hybrid marker at all, and UF/IFAS (HS1500) gives a full taxonomic-authority-cited binomial, "Citrus sinensis (L.) Osbeck," also with no hybrid marker, treating it as a settled accepted species rather than an unstable hybrid. That is a genuine disagreement about accepted taxonomic treatment (hybrid-with-parentage-and-no-authority vs. species-with-a-named-authority), not a cosmetic "x" vs "×" notation difference, so scientific_name_accepted is left null rather than picking a side.
unknowns: scientific_name_accepted / name_note: see name_note -- NC State and Missouri Botanical Garden treat this as a hybrid with an x/× marker and stated mandarin×pomelo parentage, while RHS gives the plain binomial with no marker and UF/IFAS (HS1500) gives a full authority-cited name 'Citrus sinensis (L.) Osbeck' with no marker. A genuine disagreement about accepted taxonomic treatment, so left null.

toxicity_detail: NC State's structured poison-symptom/toxic-principle text (essential oils, psoralens, geraniol, citral, d-limonene; 'The fruit is edible, skins and plant material can cause problems') is filed specifically under a 'Poisonous to Humans:' section header, not attributed to pets -- per the rule against blending human-scoped toxicity narrative into a pet toxicity_detail, that text was not used, even though toxic_to_pets=true is independently supported by NC State's own 'Problem for Cats'/'Problem for Dogs' tags. RHS's toxicity note ('Fruit harmful to skin with sunlight/skin allergen') is also unusable here because RHS explicitly scopes it to '(lemon and lime-bearing Citrus only)', i.e. RHS itself excludes Citrus sinensis (orange) from that claim. No admissible source gives a pet-specific toxicity narrative for orange (naming which part -- peel/leaf/stem vs. edible pulp -- is dangerous to cats/dogs specifically), so toxicity_detail stays null despite toxic_to_pets=true being confirmed via the tags alone.

day_f_min/day_f_max/night_f_min/night_f_max: Clemson's Container Citrus Production factsheet (anchored to sweet orange via its 'C. sinensis -- Navel and Valencia' mention) gives 'Optimum temperatures for fruit production are between 65 °F and 85 °F' and 'Most citrus trees can tolerate cooler temperatures, down to around 50 °F', but both sentences are phrased for 'citrus trees'/'citrus' generically, not sweet orange specifically, and neither splits day vs. night. UMD's 'Growing Dwarf Citrus' gives an explicit day/night split (65-75°F day, 55-65°F night) but never names orange at all among the dwarf citrus types it covers ('lemons and limes to mandarins and kumquats'), so it was excluded entirely rather than used with a nonexistent species anchor. Left null.

humidity_need/humidity_pct_min/humidity_pct_max: sole supporting sentence ('At least 8 hours of sunlight and high humidity, 30% to 60%, are required for optimum growth and development') is from the same Clemson factsheet, phrased generically for 'citrus' rather than sweet orange specifically. Left null.
light_fc_min/light_fc_good: no admissible source gives light levels in footcandles; all give hours of direct sun instead.

direct_sun_hours_max: NC State says 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)' and Clemson says 'At least 8 hours of sunlight' -- both are stated minimum thresholds ('or more'/'at least'), not a maximum, so no defensible max-hours figure exists.

soil_base: RHS recommends 'a container of peat-free, loam-based potting compost with added grit'; Clemson recommends '4 parts shredded aged pine bark and 1 part peat moss or coir (cocoa fiber)'. Neither maps cleanly to a fixed enum value (standard_potting, chunky_aroid, cactus_succulent, etc.), so left null rather than forcing a fit.

soil_drainage: NC State's structured field reads 'Soil Drainage: Good Drainage, Moist' -- this describes well-drained, moist soil but doesn't literally state a drainage-speed category ('fast' vs 'moderate' vs 'moisture_retentive'), so left null rather than guessing which enum term the quote supports.

soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max: the only prose 'pH of 5-6' sentence on NC State's orange page ('It prefers a pH of 5 - 6 but will tolerate a neutral or alkaline range as well') was checked against NC State's own Citrus x limon (lemon) page and found to be word-for-word identical boilerplate reused verbatim across both species pages -- exactly the cross-species reused-text pattern the brief warns about -- so it was not trusted as orange-specific. NC State's and RHS's structured pH fields are both categorical only (Acid/Neutral/Alkaline; 'Acid or Neutral') with no numeric bounds. Clemson gives two different numeric ranges in two different factsheets (5.5-6.5 in Container Citrus Production, 6.0-6.5 in In-Ground Citrus Production) and UF/IFAS HS132 gives 5.5-6.5, but every one of those sentences is phrased for 'citrus'/'citrus trees' generically, not sweet orange specifically, and the two Clemson figures for citrus don't even agree with each other. No orange-specific numeric pH source was found, so left null.

water_dry_down_target: no source states a specific dry-down depth/target description distinct from the check-depth guidance already reflected qualitatively in water_regime; left null rather than duplicating that guidance into an unverified target string.

water_check_depth_cm: Clemson's Container Citrus Production factsheet gives the check depth in inches ('check the top 2 to 3 inches of the soil'), not centimeters. Converting inches to a centimeter figure would introduce a number not literally present in the quote, so left null.

water_growing_days_est/water_dormant_days_est: the same Clemson factsheet says potted citrus 'will need to be watered almost daily' during heat, but this is an extreme-heat scenario, not a stated general growing-season interval, and no admissible source gives a day-interval figure for typical conditions or for dormancy. Left null.
water_estimate_basis: not addressed by any admissible source.

fertilize_active_months/fertilize_interval_days/fertilize_strength: Clemson recommends 'a slow-release fertilizer, such as a 12-6-6 or a 12-4-6' with '2 to 3 applications' during the growing season, and RHS says to 'Apply fertilisers formulated for citrus, throughout the year.' Neither source names specific calendar months, states a numeric day-interval, or gives a strength/dilution instruction, so all three fields are left null.

chill_damage_f (context, not blended into the single value): Missouri Botanical Garden's Washington navel orange profile separately advises protecting 'young trees and new growth on mature trees in the spring if temperatures fall below 32°F' -- a different, milder threshold for a more cold-sensitive plant stage than UF/IFAS's 28°F mature-fruit-damage figure used for chill_damage_f. These aren't a genuine cross-source disagreement so much as guidance for different plant parts/stages (similar to UF/IFAS's own multiple lemon thresholds), so 28°F (the more explicit, species-named 'Oranges are usually damaged...' statement) was used, with the 32°F young-growth figure noted here rather than blended in. Separately, RHS's own hardiness badge for this species is 'H2: tolerant of low temperatures, but not surviving being frozen (1 to 5)' in °C -- a survival/frost-tolerance rating, not a damage-onset figure, so per the field's own definition it was not used for chill_damage_f, though it is broadly consistent with the 28-32°F figures above.

water_regime: NC State's more general statement ('It is drought tolerant but flourishes when kept moist. Do not overwater.') is compatible with, but less specific/actionable than, Clemson's check-the-surface-before-watering procedure used as the primary support for water_regime=dry_surface_between; NC State's sentence was treated as supporting context rather than the determining citation.

scientific_name_accepted — removed on audit: The value is the JSON string "null" (quoted text) rather than the actual JSON null literal -- a direct violation of structural check 6, which explicitly warns against the string "null" standing in for real null. This is a reportable defect independent of whether the underlying decision to leave it unresolved was sound. On the substance: I fetched all four sources live and confirmed the name_note's quotes are accurate -- NC State's page is titled 'Citrus x sinensis' and states 'It is a hybrid resulting from a cross between a mandarin orange and a pomelo although when this was done is not fully known' (verified verbatim); MoBot's page is titled 'Citrus × sinensis 'Washington'' and states the hybrid mandarin/pomelo parentage verbatim (down to a reproduced 'and and' typo, confirming a genuine unparaphrased copy); RHS's page title is verbatim 'Citrus sinensis | sweet orange' with no hybrid marker; UF/IFAS HS1500 verbatim cites 'Citrus sinensis (L.) Osbeck'. So a real, documented cross-source naming-convention conflict exists and this isn't under-researched -- but the field must actually be JSON null, not the string "null".

water_regime — removed on audit: The only citation supporting dry_surface_between is Clemson's Container Citrus Production line 'check the top 2 to 3 inches of the soil' (verified live), which is phrased for potted citrus generically -- it never names orange or Citrus sinensis. The record itself explicitly disqualifies this identical factsheet's generic 'citrus'/'citrus trees' phrasing as insufficiently species-specific for day_f_min/max, night_f_min/max, and humidity_pct_min/max, using the exact same 'C. sinensis - Navel and Valencia' context-anchor citation that's invoked here to justify treating the document as orange-specific. Applying the record's own stated standard consistently, water_regime has no citation that clears the bar it set for itself, so this field should have been left null instead of populated from the one available generic citation.

cool_rest_note — removed on audit: The note's sole support is Clemson's 'citrus trees can be placed in a room with southern exposure...Maintain the temperature between 55 F and 65 F' (verified live) -- phrased for 'citrus trees' generically, not Citrus sinensis specifically. This is the same defect pattern the record used to justify excluding temperature/humidity fields sourced from this identical document elsewhere in the same record. No other citation supports this note, so by the record's own internal standard it rests on disqualified generic phrasing.

RHS's grow-your-own guide gives only a germination minimum ('at least 15°C (59°F) is needed to germinate') and the separate cold-injury/bolting threshold used for chill_damage_f, neither of which is a day-growing range. Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder gives 'Best growing season temperatures fall within the range of 60-75 degrees F,' but that page is specifically for the cultivated variety Apium graveolens var. dulce, a narrower infraspecific taxon than the species-level binomial given for this record, so it was not used to avoid a taxon mismatch.
night_f_min / night_f_max: no admissible source gives nighttime temperature figures for this species.
cool_rest_note: no admissible source describes a dormancy/chilling-rest requirement for this species (as distinct from the cold-injury/bolting threshold captured in chill_damage_f).
humidity_need / humidity_pct_min / humidity_pct_max: no admissible source addresses ambient humidity for this species.
light_fc_min / light_fc_good: no admissible source gives footcandle figures; sources give only the categorical 'full sun' / 'partial shade' terms.

direct_sun_hours_max: NC State defines 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)' with no stated upper limit, and RHS's Position field ('Full sun, Partial shade') likewise gives no numeric ceiling; no source states how many hours of direct sun celery tolerates beyond the full-sun minimum.

soil_ph is well supported numerically by NC State ('Neutral (6.0-8.0)'), but note RHS's own Growing Conditions box separately lists the much broader categorical 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' for pH -- not a numeric conflict, but the broader RHS category was not used to override NC State's specific range.

soil_drainage: RHS's own quick-reference Growing Conditions box lists 'Moist but well–drained or Poorly–drained,' a broad, generic-sounding pairing. RHS's own detailed grow-your-own narrative is more specific and repeats across multiple sections that celery's wild ancestor grows on 'boggy riversides and marshy ground,' needs 'moisture-retentive soil that never dries out,' warns that 'very free-draining soil' is unsuitable, and states 'the soil should never be allowed to dry out.' The specific, repeated narrative was used (moisture_retentive) over the generic box entry.

water_check_depth_cm / water_dry_down_target / water_growing_days_est / water_dormant_days_est / water_estimate_basis: no admissible source gives numeric watering-interval, check-depth, or dormancy-duration figures for this species.

fertilize_interval_days / fertilize_active_months / fertilize_strength: RHS's Feeding section gives an interval for pot-grown celery only as 'feed every fortnight with a balanced liquid fertiliser through the summer' -- a named-unit phrase equivalent to 14 days, but the digits '14' never literally appear in the quote, so per the literal-numeral rule for citation labels this was left null rather than converted from the named unit. RHS names only the season 'summer,' not specific calendar months, and gives no dilution/strength figure for the liquid fertiliser either. Separately, RHS's guidance for garden-grown (non-container) celery is only a conditional single application ('a light dressing of a high nitrogen fertiliser in summer, once the plants are established') with no interval number at all.

is_houseplant: no admissible source frames Apium graveolens as an indoor container/houseplant subject for long-term growing, and no source gives a specific quote naming it 'not a houseplant.' Every source that discusses cultivation (RHS's grow-your-own guide, NC State's Cultural Conditions attributes) frames it as an outdoor garden or field vegetable -- garden-bed preparation, trenching/blanching, and even RHS's container-growing instructions describe positioning pots outdoors ('a sunny, sheltered location'). Set to false on that basis (consistent with how other garden-vegetable records in this catalog set is_houseplant without a dedicated citation) rather than a single explicit disqualifying quote.

is_houseplant — removed on audit: The field is populated (false) but has zero citations whose claim label contains 'is_houseplant' — none of the 13 citations reference this field at all. Per structural check 1, every non-null field (except scientific_name_given) must trace to at least one citation labeled for it. The record's own 'unknowns' entry for is_houseplant admits this is inferred reasoning ('consistent with how other garden-vegetable records in this catalog set is_houseplant... rather than a single explicit disqualifying quote') rather than a sourced claim, which confirms the gap rather than curing it. WebFetch of the NC State page confirms it contains no indoor/houseplant language of any kind to cite.

name_note — removed on audit: Citation 5's claim label asserts celery is the 'wild ancestor of cultivated Celery (var. dulce) and Celery Root (var. rapaceum),' but the cited NC State quote only says 'It is a wild relative of domesticated Celery... and Celery Root...' — 'relative' (kinship) is not the same claim as 'ancestor' (direct lineage), and WebFetch of the live NC State page confirms the exact wording is 'wild relative,' not 'ancestor.' The name_note body text goes further, stating Apium graveolens 'is also the wild ancestor from which the cultivated variety groups... were bred' — this stronger 'bred' framing does exist verbatim in the citations array ('from which cultivated varieties have been bred,' RHS), but that quote is tagged to a different field's claim label (citation 9, 'soil_drainage moisture_retentive'), not to name_note. Per the field-tracing rule, a citation must be labeled for the field it supports; no citation labeled 'name_note' actually contains the 'bred'/ancestor language, so that portion of name_note is effectively uncited beyond the weaker 'wild relative' quote.

Poison Hemlock -- "the plant that killed Socrates" -- confirmed toxic_to_pets=true with clean cat/dog evidence, while multiple horse/cattle/"all animals"-scoped dose figures from Penn State and UGA were correctly excluded per this catalog's cat/dog scoping rule; its well-documented confusion with edible look-alikes (wild carrot/Queen Anne's Lace, parsley, celery) was captured in unknowns even though there's no dedicated field for it.
